 A Millionaire Says GTA 6 Is Actually a Smart Financial Investment. Here’s His Reasoning.
 Gadget Review Follow Annemarije de Boer Tue, November 3, 2026 at 4:01 PM UTC Add to Preferred Sources Tue, November 3, 2026 at 4:01 PM UTC Image: Instagram/marktilbury Spending $100 to save $5,000 sounds like something you'd see on a late-night infomercial. Mark Tilbury , a British entrepreneur and social-media educator, posted a tongue-in-cheek video making exactly that argument about Grand Theft Auto VI , drawing wide attention across gaming and entertainment coverage.
 The pitch is simple: buy the game, skip the bar, pocket the difference.
 How $99.99 Becomes $1.25
 Tilbury's math starts at the register and works backward from there. 
 Advertisement Advertisement Tilbury's calculation starts with the reported $99.99 price of the Ultimate Edition and divides it by an estimated 80-hour campaign . That produces an entertainment cost of roughly $1.25 per hour , according to his figures.
 Those playtime estimates come from Tilbury, not from Rockstar or Take-Two. Treat them as assumptions, not developer guarantees.
 The 200-Hour Extension
 Factor in the open world, and the cost per hour falls further. 
 Factor in side missions and open-world exploration, Tilbury argues, and total playtime could reach around 200 hours . At that volume, cost per hour drops to about 50 cents.
 Four hours of play per evening across 200 hours works out to 50 evenings.
 Where the $5,000 Comes From
 The headline figure is a rhetorical comparison, not a verified saving. 
 Advertisement Advertisement Tilbury compares those 50 evenings with 50 nights out at $100 each, producing a $5,000 alternative-spending figure. The actual arithmetic gap between $5,000 and $99.99 is closer to $4,900, but Tilbury frames the difference rhetorically as "saving $5,000."
 "That's why buying GTA 6 actually saves you $5,000." Mark Tilbury, entrepreneur and social-media educator, as reported by IGN.
 That framing is the joke. The math behind it is real enough.
 What the Calculation Requires You to Believe
 The comparison rests on two assumptions that many players will not share. 
 The comparison holds only if every alternative evening costs exactly $100 and if gaming and going out are mutually exclusive activities. Opportunity costs , such as time away from work, relationships, or other pursuits, do not appear anywhere in the equation.
 Advertisement Advertisement For many players, the actual alternative to a gaming session is a streaming service, not ordering rounds until last call.
 The Pricing Question That Actually Matters
 The numbers Tilbury uses have broader implications beyond the joke. 
 Available reports list the Standard Edition at $79.99 and the Ultimate Edition at $99.99 ; those figures should be verified against official Rockstar or Take-Two announcements before treating them as confirmed. The distinction between reported and confirmed matters here. Some industry figures have argued that GTA 6 could encourage publishers to charge more for major releases, and the edition prices are central to that conversation.
 Why That Precedent Has Limits
 Rockstar's position in the market is unusual, and its pricing power reflects that. 
 Advertisement Advertisement Rockstar operates at a scale that most studios cannot approach, with decades of franchise recognition, a global audience, and a production budget that few publishers can match. A premium price that makes sense for one of the most anticipated releases in gaming history does not automatically apply to untested intellectual properties. Shorter games from independent developers face a very different commercial reality.
 Price Is Not the Same as Value
 Whether the math works depends entirely on the player doing it. 
 The cost-per-hour argument may appear compelling for players who sink 200-plus hours into the open world or continue playing after finishing the campaign. For someone who buys it, plays for ten hours, and loses interest, the math looks very different.
 Tilbury's video is entertainment commentary, not financial advice. Whether the game earns its price depends entirely on how much of it you actually play.
